landmarks.name: Petra
landmarks.writeup: An ancient Nabatean city famous for its rock-cut architecture and water conduit system.

wiki.extract: Petra, originally known to its inhabitants as Raqmu, is an ancient city and archaeological site in southern Jordan. Famous for its rock-cut architecture and water conduit systems, Petra is also called the "Rose City" because of the colour of the sandstone from which it is carved. The city is one of the New 7 Wonders of the World and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

landmarks.name: Wadi Rum
landmarks.writeup: A protected desert wilderness known for its dramatic sandstone mountains and prehistoric rock art.

wiki.extract: Wadi Rum (Arabic: وادي رم Wādī Ramm, also Wādī al-Ramm, known also as the Valley of the Moon or Red mountains, is a valley cut into the sandstone and granite rock in southern Jordan, near the border with Saudi Arabia and about 60 km to the east of the city of Aqaba. With an area of 720 km2 it is the largest wadi in Jordan.

landmarks.name: Dead Sea
landmarks.writeup: The lowest point on earth, famous for its hypersaline water and therapeutic properties.

wiki.extract: The Dead Sea, also known by other names, is a landlocked salt lake bordered by Jordan to the east, the West Bank to the west and Israel to the southwest. It lies in the endorheic basin of the Jordan Rift Valley, and its main tributary is the Jordan River.

landmarks.name: Amman Citadel
landmarks.writeup: A historic site in the capital city featuring ruins from various civilizations including Roman and Umayyad.

wiki.extract: The Amman Citadel on Citadel Hill is an archaeological site on an L-shaped hill towering over Downtown Amman, in the central part of the capital of Jordan.

landmarks.name: Jerash
landmarks.writeup: One of the best-preserved Roman provincial towns with extensive ruins including theaters and temples.

wiki.extract: Jerash or Jarash is a city in northern Jordan. The city is the administrative center of the Jerash Governorate, and has a population of 50,745 as of 2015. It is located 30.0 miles north of the capital city Amman.

cultural_events.name: Jerash Festival
cultural_events.writeup: An annual cultural festival showcasing traditional music, dance, and arts in the ancient city of Jerash.

wiki.extract: The Jerash Festival for Culture and Arts is an annual event held in Jerash, Jordan. It is part of the Jordan Festival, which aims to enrich cultural activities in Jordan. Founded in 1981 by Queen Noor, it features several shows performed by Jordanian, Arab and foreign artists.

cultural_events.name: Amman International Theatre Festival
cultural_events.writeup: A festival promoting theatrical arts with performances from local and international groups.

wiki.extract: Roman Theatre of Amman is a 6,000-seat, 2nd-century Roman theatre. A famous landmark in the Jordanian capital, it dates back to the Roman period when the city was known as Philadelphia. The theatre and the nearby Odeon are flanking the new Hashemite Plaza from the south and the east respectively, while the Roman Nymphaeum is just a short stroll away in north-westerly direction.

cultural_events.writeup: A multi-disciplinary arts festival held in Amman featuring music, dance, and visual arts.

food_writeup: Jordanian cuisine features dishes like mansaf (lamb cooked in fermented dried yogurt), falafel, hummus, and fresh bread, reflecting a rich Levantine culinary tradition.
brief_history: Jordan has a history dating back to ancient civilizations including the Nabateans and Romans. It became an independent kingdom in 1946 and has since played a key role in Middle Eastern politics.

commentary.inflation_management: The dinar's peg to the US dollar (since 1995) anchors Jordanian monetary policy, and inflation has been moderate outside commodity shocks: 14.0% in 2008 on the global spike, then mostly 1-5%, with mild deflation in 2015-16 and a 2022 peak of only 4.2%. The IMF projects 1.8% for 2025. The Central Bank of Jordan follows the Fed, which has at times meant tight policy during domestic weakness. Fuel-price liberalization episodes (notably 2012) caused step increases but did not de-anchor expectations.
commentary.debt_management: Public debt has climbed relentlessly from 60.0% of GDP in 2006 to a projected 82.8% in 2025, with no sustained reversal. Drivers include chronic deficits, the fiscal cost of hosting over a million Syrian refugees, energy-import dependence, and repeated shocks (Arab Spring, COVID, regional wars). The ratio dipped to 47.9% in 2008 on strong growth but the trend since has been upward, with COVID lifting it from 69.4% (2019) to 77.9% (2020). Successive IMF programs have imposed gradual consolidation, but the debt path remains upward-sloping.

key_events.event: Commodity spike drove inflation to 14.0%; debt briefly fell on strong growth.
Arab Spring protests; fuel-subsidy cuts in 2012 sparked unrest but restored some fiscal space.
Syrian refugee influx strained public services and the budget.
COVID-19 pushed debt to 77.9% of GDP; new IMF program agreed.
Ukraine-war commodity shock lifted inflation to 4.2%; tourism recovered.
Gaza war hurt tourism and trade; debt kept climbing to 82.8% projected for 2025.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: Jordan's outlook is constrained: debt is on an unsustainable trajectory without faster growth or deeper consolidation, and the economy is highly exposed to regional instability. IMF-backed reforms (tax, energy pricing) offer a path to stabilize debt, and tourism and ICT services provide upside. Water scarcity is a binding long-run constraint. Analytical assessment: muddling through with donor and IMF support is the base case; a regional escalation that hits tourism or aid would force sharper adjustment.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
